goals: State the standard meaning of a right and the test that separates a right from a want
Explain natural, human and legal rights as sources of rights
Describe political, civil, economic and cultural rights with examples
Explain why a clean environment, privacy and the rights of children and indigenous peoples are increasingly recognised claims
Plan a five mark answer on sources and kinds of rights

slides.heading: Rights: Meaning, Sources and Kinds
slides.body_md: Part 1: what a **right** is, where rights come from, and the **kinds** of rights.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what a right is, want or right, sources, kinds and newer claims
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: People make many claims on one another and on the state. Which of them are rights? In this part we learn what a right is, how to tell a right from a want, where rights come from, and the main kinds of rights.

slides.heading: What a right is

rows: Standard definition
An entitlement or justified claim, recognised by society and usually by law, that lets a person live with dignity and freedom
A claim on others
A right places a duty on others, including the state, to respect it
Why it matters
Rights protect the conditions of a dignified life for every person
Imagined case
In Pelham every child may attend the town school, and the town must not turn a child away

visual.alt: Table on the meaning of a right: an entitlement or justified claim recognised by society and usually by law that lets a person live with dignity and freedom; it places a duty on others including the state; it protects the conditions of a dignified life; in imagined Pelham every child may attend the town school and the town must not turn a child away
visual.caption: Pelham is imagined.

slides.narration: A right is an entitlement or justified claim. Society recognises it, usually through law, and it lets a person live with dignity and freedom. Because a right is a claim on others, it places a duty on them, including the state, to respect it. In imagined Pelham, the town must not turn a child away from school.

slides.heading: What is not a right

rows: A want
Not every want is a right, however strongly it is felt
The test
A claim becomes a right when it is necessary for a dignified life and accepted as justified
Equal application
It must be able to apply equally to all, not to one person or family only
Imagined case
A new phone each year is a want; safe drinking water is a claim that meets the test

slides.narration: Not every want is a right. A claim becomes a right when it is necessary for a dignified life and is accepted as justified. It must also be able to apply equally to all. A new phone each year is a want. Safe drinking water is a claim that meets the test.

slides.narration: This flow gives a test. First ask whether the claim is needed for a life of dignity and freedom. Then ask whether society can accept it as justified. Then ask whether it can apply equally to all persons. If every answer is yes, the claim is a right. If any answer is no, it is a want or a preference.

visual.alt: Chart of the three sources of rights. Natural rights are an idea of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries that people hold rights by nature, associated with Locke and the rights to life, liberty and property. Human rights are the rights all persons have because they are human, and the United Nations declaration of 1948 is the best-known statement. Legal rights are recognised and protected by law and the state, and constitutions often list them, as the Indian Fundamental Rights do. Natural and human rights give reasons for a claim, and legal rights make the claim enforceable by the state
visual.caption: Three sources of rights.

slides.narration: This chart shows three sources. Natural rights are said to belong to people by nature. Human rights belong to all persons because they are human. Legal rights are recognised and protected by law and the state. Natural and human rights give reasons for a claim, and legal rights make it enforceable.

People are said to have certain rights by nature, apart from any government

Associated with

slides.heading: Human rights

Rights all persons have because they are human
No condition

Best-known statement
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948
Imagined case
A campaigner in Belmora asks for safe working conditions that no law yet mentions

notes.title: Rights: Notes

sections.heading: 1. What a right is; want or right
sections.body_md:
A **right** is an entitlement or **justified claim**, recognised by society and usually by law, that allows a person to live with **dignity and freedom** and places a **duty** on others, including the state, to respect it.

Not every **want** is a right. A claim becomes a right when it is **necessary for a dignified life**, is **accepted as justified**, and can **apply equally to all**.

A wish or preference that is not necessary for a dignified life and cannot be justified as a claim for all.
The worth that every person has simply as a person.

sections.heading: 2. Sources of rights
sections.body_md:
Rights are traced to three sources.

- **Natural rights**: the seventeenth and eighteenth century idea that people have rights by nature, for example the rights to **life, liberty and property** associated with John Locke.
- **Human rights**: rights all persons have because they are human. The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** (United Nations, 1948) is the best-known statement.
- **Legal rights**: rights recognised and protected by law and the state. Constitutions often list them, as the Indian Constitution does in its Fundamental Rights.

Rights that all persons have because they are human, whatever their country, caste, religion or gender.
Rights that are recognised and protected by law and enforced by the state.

sections.heading: 3. Kinds of rights
sections.body_md:
Rights are also grouped by what they protect.

- **Political rights**: to vote, to contest elections, to form parties.
- **Civil liberties**: freedom of expression, a fair trial.
- **Economic rights**: basic needs, a minimum wage, livelihood.
- **Cultural rights**: to preserve one's language and culture, and education in the mother tongue.

key_terms.definition_md: Rights that let people take part in government, such as to vote, to contest elections and to form parties.
Rights that protect personal freedom and fair treatment, such as freedom of expression and a fair trial.
Rights that secure a livelihood and basic needs, such as a minimum wage.
Rights that let a group keep and develop its way of life, such as preserving a language and culture and education in the mother tongue.

sections.body_md: A right is a claim, so it places **duties on the state**. The duty of the state not to violate a right.

sections.heading: 6. Responsibilities of individuals; limits on rights
sections.body_md:
Individuals should **respect the rights of others**, **balance** their rights when these clash with others' rights (for example freedom of expression against privacy), **care for shared goods** such as the environment, and **be vigilant** when governments restrict rights in the name of security. On the last point, some argue that restrictions can last or grow and must be watched; others argue that a real threat may justify reasonable limits for a time.

Rights are **not absolute**. **Reasonable limits** protect the rights of others and the common good.

A restriction on a right that is clear, announced, applies to all, protects others or the common good, and leaves the right in place.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling every want a right: apply the test of necessity, justification and equal application.
- Mixing sources with kinds: natural, human and legal are sources; political, civil, economic and cultural are kinds.
- Listing kinds without examples: give one example of each.
- Saying newer claims are settled everywhere: write that they are increasingly recognised.
- Saying rights place duties only on the state: individuals have responsibilities too.
- Saying rights are unlimited: reasonable limits protect others and the common good.
- Taking a side on security: give both views with reasons, then a test for judging a restriction.

**Tips:** add an imagined example to each point; for a clash of rights, name the two claims, weigh the harm and propose a reasonable limit; end with a reasoned judgement.

cards.back_md: An entitlement or justified claim, recognised by society and usually by law, that lets a person live with dignity and freedom and places a duty on others to respect it.
No: a claim is a right only if it is necessary for a dignified life, accepted as justified, and able to apply equally to all.

cards.back_md: Necessary for a dignified life; accepted as justified; able to apply equally to all.
The worth that every person has simply as a person.

questions.stem_md: In political theory, a right is best defined as

options.text_md: any wish that a person happens to have
a justified claim, recognised by society and usually by law, that lets a person live with dignity and freedom and places a duty on others to respect it
a favour that a ruler may grant or withdraw at will
a duty that only the state has to perform

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a justified claim, recognised by society and usually by law, that lets a person live with dignity and freedom and places a duty on others to respect it. A right is an entitlement or justified claim that society recognises, usually through law, and it places a duty on others. A passing wish, a ruler's favour and a duty of the state alone do not describe it.

questions.stem_md: Which feature best separates a right from a mere want?

options.text_md: A want is always more costly than a right
A right is whatever a majority happens to desire at a given time
A want is any claim that a person says aloud
A right is a claim that is necessary for a dignified life, is accepted as justified, and can apply equally to all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A right is a claim that is necessary for a dignified life, is accepted as justified, and can apply equally to all. A claim becomes a right when it is needed for a dignified life, is accepted as justified and can apply equally to all. Cost, the desire of a majority and the act of saying a claim aloud do not decide the matter.

questions.stem_md: Chetan of the imagined town of Pelham says that he has a right to a new phone every year because all his friends get one. Applying the test of a justified claim that is needed for a dignified life, which response is best?

options.text_md: A new phone each year is a want; it is not necessary for a dignified life, so it does not meet the test of a right
It is a right, since Chetan wants it strongly
It is a right, since his friends get one
It is a right, since anything modern is a right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A new phone each year is a want; it is not necessary for a dignified life, so it does not meet the test of a right. The claim fails the test because a yearly phone is not necessary for a life of dignity and freedom. Strength of desire, what friends have and the novelty of an item do not turn a want into a right.

questions.stem_md: Natural rights are best described as

options.text_md: rights that exist only after a legislature passes an Act
rights granted to the citizens of one state alone by its ruler
rights that people are said to have by nature, before and apart from any government or law
rights that belong only to those who own property

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** rights that people are said to have by nature, before and apart from any government or law. The idea of natural rights holds that people have certain rights by nature. Rights that exist only after an Act, rights granted by a ruler to citizens and rights tied to property ownership are different ideas.

questions.stem_md: Which set of natural rights is associated with the thinker John Locke?

options.text_md: Wealth, fame and power
Equal income, rest and leisure
Life, liberty and property
Voting, taxation and military service

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Life, liberty and property. Locke is linked with natural rights to life, liberty and property. The other sets are not the rights associated with him.

questions.stem_md: Human rights are best described as rights that

options.text_md: every person has because he or she is a human being, whatever his or her country, caste, religion or gender
a state gives only to its own citizens
belong only to adults who have the vote
exist only when a court has declared them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** every person has because he or she is a human being, whatever his or her country, caste, religion or gender. Human rights belong to all persons simply because they are human. They are not limited to citizens, to voters, or to cases that a court has already declared.

questions.stem_md: The best-known international statement of human rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948, is the

options.text_md: Treaty of Versailles
Magna Carta
Kyoto Protocol
Universal Declaration of Human Rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations in 1948. The Treaty of Versailles ended a war, Magna Carta is a medieval charter, and the Kyoto Protocol deals with climate.

questions.stem_md: Legal rights differ from natural rights mainly because legal rights are

options.text_md: held only by ancient peoples
recognised and protected by law and enforced by the state
never written down anywhere
the same thing as wants

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** recognised and protected by law and enforced by the state. Legal rights are recognised and protected by law, and the state enforces them. They are not restricted to ancient peoples, they are often written in constitutions, and they differ from wants.

questions.stem_md: The imagined constitution of Karvale lists freedom of speech, a fair trial and the vote, and its courts protect them. As to their source, these rights are best called

options.text_md: legal rights, since a constitution recognises them and the state protects them
natural rights only, since no law can ever recognise them
wants, since they appear on a list
duties, since a constitution lists them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** legal rights, since a constitution recognises them and the state protects them. Rights written into a constitution and protected by courts are legal rights. A constitution can recognise rights, a listed right is not a mere want, and a right is not a duty.

questions.stem_md: A campaigner in imagined Belmora says that the country's farm labourers deserve safe working conditions even though Belmora's laws do not yet mention them, because every person is entitled to this as a human being. Her claim rests mainly on the idea of

options.text_md: legal rights, since the law already protects the claim
human rights, which do not depend on the law of any one country
a want that fails every test
political rights to contest elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** human rights, which do not depend on the law of any one country. She appeals to what people are owed as human beings, which is the idea of human rights, and she does so because the law is silent. The claim is not yet a legal right, and it is not about elections.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Orsolin, a group of citizens registers a new party and puts up candidates in a council election. Which kind of right are they using?

options.text_md: Economic rights, to a minimum wage
Cultural rights, to keep a language
Political rights, to form parties and contest elections
Civil liberties, to a fair trial

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Political rights, to form parties and contest elections. Forming a party and contesting an election are political rights. A minimum wage is economic, language is cultural, and a fair trial is a civil liberty.

questions.stem_md: A newspaper in Pelham is free to publish a report that criticises the town council, and a man accused of theft there receives a public hearing before an impartial judge. Both situations involve

options.text_md: economic rights
cultural rights
the right to vote only
civil liberties

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** civil liberties. Freedom of expression and a fair trial are civil liberties. Neither situation is about wages, language or voting.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Quillon Council fixes a minimum daily wage for brick workers and starts a livelihood scheme for landless families. These measures protect

options.text_md: cultural rights
political rights
the freedom of expression
economic rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** economic rights. A minimum wage, a livelihood and basic needs are economic rights. They are not cultural or political rights, and they do not concern expression.

questions.stem_md: The imagined country of Marenia allows a minority community to run primary schools in its own language and to hold its festivals openly. Which kind of right is most directly protected?

options.text_md: Economic rights
Political rights
Cultural rights
The civil liberty of a fair trial

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Cultural rights. Preserving a language and culture, and schooling in the mother tongue, are cultural rights. The case does not concern wages, elections or trials.

questions.stem_md: Which of these claims is correctly matched with its kind of right?

options.text_md: A fair trial: an economic right
Education in one's mother tongue: a cultural right
A minimum wage: a political right
The vote: a cultural right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Education in one's mother tongue: a cultural right. Education in the mother tongue belongs with cultural rights. A fair trial is a civil liberty, a minimum wage is economic, and the vote is a political right, so the other pairs are mismatched.

questions.stem_md: A clean environment, privacy, the rights of children and the rights of indigenous peoples are best described as

options.text_md: newer claims that are increasingly recognised as rights
claims that every country has rejected
claims that have no link with dignity
rights that existed only before the seventeenth century

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** newer claims that are increasingly recognised as rights. These are newer claims that are being recognised more and more. They have not been rejected everywhere, they bear on dignity, and they are not confined to an early period.

questions.stem_md: Residents of the imagined town of Odrin say that smoke from a brick works makes the air unfit to breathe, and they ask that safe air be recognised as a claim. This claim is an example of

options.text_md: a political right to contest elections
a newer claim to a clean environment
a cultural right to a language
a claim that no country can ever treat as a right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a newer claim to a clean environment. A demand for breathable air belongs to the newer claim of a clean environment. It is not political or cultural, and some countries do recognise such claims.

questions.stem_md: A wealthy family of the imagined town of Odrin demands that only its members be allowed to fish in the town lake, and calls this its right. Why does the claim fail the test of a right?

options.text_md: Fishing is never needed by anyone
Lakes cannot be used by people
A right can be claimed only by the poor
A right must be a claim that can apply equally to all, but this claim asks for a privilege for one family

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A right must be a claim that can apply equally to all, but this claim asks for a privilege for one family. A claim becomes a right when it can be extended equally to everyone. A privilege for one family cannot, so it fails. Fishing can matter to livelihood, lakes can be used, and rights are not only for the poor.

questions.stem_md: Rights place duties on the state. Which of these shows the state refraining from violating a right?

options.text_md: Police do not arrest a person without a lawful reason
A town builds a clinic
A school is opened in a remote village
A law fixes a minimum wage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Police do not arrest a person without a lawful reason. Not arresting without lawful reason is a refraining duty. Building a clinic, opening a school and fixing a minimum wage are acts of providing conditions for rights.

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly shows one duty of the state to act and one duty of the state to refrain?

options.text_md: Act: silence a peaceful newspaper. Refrain: do not provide schools
Act and refrain both mean doing nothing
Act: provide a school in every village. Refrain: do not silence a peaceful newspaper without lawful cause
Act: ask citizens to protect rights. Refrain: nothing is required

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Act: provide a school in every village. Refrain: do not silence a peaceful newspaper without lawful cause. Providing schools is an act that creates conditions for a right, and not silencing a peaceful newspaper is a refraining duty. The other options reverse the duties, confuse them, or deny that the state has any.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a responsibility of individuals that goes with having rights?

options.text_md: Ignoring any law that one dislikes
Claiming whatever one wants
Respecting the rights of others
Leaving every duty to the state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Respecting the rights of others. Individuals are expected to respect the rights of others. Ignoring laws, claiming anything and leaving all duties to the state do not fit.

questions.stem_md: Esha's neighbour in Pelham plays a loudspeaker at full volume every evening as an exercise of his freedom of expression, while Esha needs quiet to study. Which approach best fits the idea of balancing rights?

options.text_md: Both accept reasonable limits, such as fixed hours and a lower volume, so that each right is respected
Expression always overrides study
Study always overrides expression, with no hearing
Neither person has any right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both accept reasonable limits, such as fixed hours and a lower volume, so that each right is respected. When rights clash, each side accepts reasonable limits so that both claims are respected as far as possible. One right does not always override the other, and neither side loses all rights.

questions.stem_md: Households in the imagined hamlet of Dunmere dump waste in the shared stream, saying that each family may do what it likes. Which idea do they overlook?

options.text_md: Streams belong to no one
Rights have no link with duties
Only the state may protect a stream
Individuals have a responsibility to care for shared goods such as the environment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Individuals have a responsibility to care for shared goods such as the environment. Shared goods such as water need care from the people who use them. Streams do serve people, rights are linked with responsibilities, and the duty to protect is not the state's alone.

questions.stem_md: Some people argue that citizens should be vigilant when a government restricts rights in the name of security. Which reason would they most likely give?

options.text_md: Governments never face any real threat
Restrictions, once accepted, may last or grow, so they should be reasonable, limited and open to review
Security has no value for a society
Rights should be set aside whenever the state asks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Restrictions, once accepted, may last or grow, so they should be reasonable, limited and open to review. Those who urge vigilance stress that limits should be reasonable and reviewable. Others reply that real threats can justify some limits. Denying all threats, denying the value of security or giving up rights on request is not their argument.

questions.stem_md: Why are rights described as not absolute?

options.text_md: Because reasonable limits are needed to protect the rights of others and the common good
Because rights are mere wishes
Because only the state can have rights
Because rights apply to rulers alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Because reasonable limits are needed to protect the rights of others and the common good. Rights are not absolute since reasonable limits protect other people and the common good. Rights are not wishes, individuals hold them, and they do not apply to rulers alone.

questions.stem_md: The council of imagined Marenia permits a public rally but asks that it end before dark and keep one lane of the main road clear for ambulances. Which statement best describes the condition?

options.text_md: A violation, since any limit cancels a right
A reasonable limit that protects others and the common good while the rally itself is allowed
Proof that no right to hold a rally exists
An example of an absolute right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A reasonable limit that protects others and the common good while the rally itself is allowed. The rally is allowed and the condition protects other people, so it is a reasonable limit. Not every limit cancels a right, the right still exists, and an absolute right would carry no conditions.

questions.stem_md: Which of these restrictions on a right is most likely to be seen as reasonable?

options.text_md: An order that bans all public speech in the town for a year without giving any reason
A rule that silences only those who criticise the council
A town permits a loud music festival only until ten at night so that residents can sleep, and announces the rule in advance
A rule that lets officials change the limit at will without notice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A town permits a loud music festival only until ten at night so that residents can sleep, and announces the rule in advance. A limit that is clear, announced, applies to all and protects others is reasonable. A blanket ban without reasons, a rule aimed at critics and a limit that officials may change at will are not.

questions.stem_md: A student of the imagined Pelham School says that if she has a right, someone else must have a duty. Which reasoning supports her?

options.text_md: Rights are claims against nobody
Duties exist only for those who have no rights
A right needs no recognition from society
A right is a claim on others, so recognising it places a duty on the state and on other people to respect it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A right is a claim on others, so recognising it places a duty on the state and on other people to respect it. A right is a justified claim that others must respect, so each right carries duties. A claim against nobody, duties only for the rightless, and rights without recognition do not fit the definition.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A demand for a new gadget every year is not counted as a right.

**Reason (R):** A right must be necessary for a dignified life and be accepted as justified, applying equally to all.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the gadget claim does not meet the conditions that R lays down.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Natural rights are said to belong to people whether or not a government recognises them.

**Reason (R):** Natural rights are the rights that a legislature creates when it passes a law.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: rights created by a legislature through law are legal rights, not natural rights.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A right recognised in law is usually more secure in practice than a claim made only on moral grounds.

**Reason (R):** A court of the state can enforce a legal right.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: enforcement by a court is what gives the legal right its security.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Rights are not absolute.

**Reason (R):** The exercise of a right by one person can harm the rights of others.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since one person's use of a right can harm others, reasonable limits are needed and the right is not unlimited.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Rights place duties only on the state, and individuals have none.

**Reason (R):** Individuals are expected to respect the rights of others and to care for shared goods.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: individuals also have responsibilities. R is true and states some of them, so it contradicts A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The claim to a clean environment is among the newer claims that are increasingly recognised as rights.

**Reason (R):** John Locke associated natural rights with life, liberty and property.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: Locke's list belongs to the older idea of natural rights and does not account for why new claims are being recognised.

questions.stem_md: Every want that a person feels strongly about becomes a right.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A want becomes a right only when it is necessary for a dignified life, is accepted as justified and can apply equally to all.

questions.stem_md: Human rights are the rights that all persons have because they are human.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** This is the standard meaning of human rights, which do not depend on one country's law.

questions.stem_md: A right may be used in any manner whatever, with no limit, even when its use harms other people.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Rights are not absolute, since unlimited use by one person can harm other people and the shared interest of society.

questions.stem_md: Rights oblige the state both to provide conditions in which they can be enjoyed and to refrain from violating them.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The state has duties to act, for example by providing schools, and to refrain, for example by not arresting without lawful cause.

questions.stem_md: A right is a justified ___, recognised by society and usually by law, that places a duty on others to respect it.
questions.solution_md: A right is a justified claim or entitlement that society recognises.

questions.stem_md: Rights are not ___; reasonable limits protect the rights of others and the common good.

questions.stem_md: Rights that are recognised and protected by law and enforced by the state are called ___ rights.

questions.stem_md: Match each term with its description.

options.text_md: Natural rights
Human rights
Legal rights

match_right.text_md: Held by all persons because they are human, as in a United Nations declaration of 1948

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined claim from Marenia with the kind of right it belongs to.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps in the order in which a student could test whether an imagined claim from Pelham is a right.

Ask whether society can accept the claim as justified

It places a duty on others to respect it

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between human rights and legal rights in one point each.
questions.solution_md: One point each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Human rights** are held by every person simply because he or she is human, whether or not a country's law mentions them. **Legal rights** are recognised and protected by law, and the state enforces them, as constitutions often list.

marking_scheme.step: Human rights: held because one is human
Legal rights: recognised and enforced by law and the state

questions.stem_md: Name any two kinds of rights and give one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Two kinds with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: **Political rights** include the right to vote and to contest elections. **Economic rights** include a minimum wage and a means of livelihood. Civil liberties such as freedom of expression and cultural rights such as education in one's mother tongue are also kinds of rights.

marking_scheme.step: A second kind with an example

questions.stem_md: Name two newer claims that are increasingly recognised as rights, and say why they are called claims.
questions.solution_md: Two claims and why.

answer.model_answer_md: Two examples are the right to a **clean environment** and the right to **privacy**; the rights of children and of indigenous peoples are others. They are called **claims** because societies are still debating and recognising them more and more.

questions.stem_md: State the two kinds of duty that rights place on the state, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Act and refrain.

answer.model_answer_md: Rights oblige the state to **act**, for example by opening schools and clinics that provide the conditions for rights. They also oblige it to **refrain**, for example by not arresting a person without a lawful reason.

marking_scheme.step: Duty to act, with an example
Duty to refrain, with an example

questions.stem_md: State any two responsibilities of individuals that go with rights.
questions.solution_md: Two responsibilities.

answer.model_answer_md: Individuals should **respect the rights of others**, so that using one's own right does not harm another. They should also **care for shared goods** such as the environment, and balance their rights when these clash with the rights of others.

marking_scheme.step: Another responsibility, such as caring for shared goods

questions.stem_md: Two students of the imagined Pelham School clash: one wants to practise drums in the common hall at noon, another wants quiet there to study. Suggest one way to balance the two claims and say why it is fair.
questions.solution_md: A balancing arrangement and the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: The school could set **fixed hours**: drums at one time, quiet at another, or use a separate room. This is **fair** because each student's claim is respected within a **reasonable limit** and neither loses the right entirely.

marking_scheme.step: A workable arrangement such as fixed hours or a separate room
Fair because each claim is respected within reasonable limits

questions.stem_md: Explain why rights are not absolute and give one example of a reasonable limit.
questions.solution_md: Reason and example.

answer.model_answer_md: Rights are not **absolute** because using a right without limit can harm the **rights of others** and the common good. A reasonable limit is a rule that a loud festival must end at night so that residents can sleep.

marking_scheme.step: Unlimited use could harm others and the common good
A suitable example of a reasonable limit

questions.stem_md: Explain the three sources of rights, with one point on each.
questions.solution_md: Natural, human and legal.

answer.model_answer_md: **Natural rights** are said to belong to people by nature, as in the seventeenth and eighteenth century idea linked with Locke. **Human rights** belong to all persons because they are human, and a United Nations declaration of 1948 is the best-known statement. **Legal rights** are recognised and protected by law and the state, as constitutions often list.

questions.stem_md: Name the kind of right in each imagined case: (i) a farm labourer of Marenia asks for a minimum wage; (ii) a minority of Orsolin asks for primary schooling in its own language; (iii) a citizen of Karvale stands for election. Give a reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Kind and reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The farm labourer's claim is an **economic right**, since a minimum wage secures a livelihood and basic needs. (ii) The minority's claim is a **cultural right**, since schooling in the mother tongue helps to preserve a language and culture. (iii) The citizen's claim is a **political right**, since contesting an election is a way of taking part in government.

questions.stem_md: Why are claims such as privacy and the rights of children described as increasingly recognised rather than settled everywhere? Give a reason and an example.
questions.solution_md: Changing needs and uneven recognition.

answer.model_answer_md: As societies change, people raise new claims that they see as needed for a **dignified life**, such as **privacy** in a digital age or protection for **children**. Countries recognise these claims at different times and in different ways, so they are **increasingly recognised** but not yet settled everywhere.

marking_scheme.step: New needs lead to new claims
An example such as privacy or children
Recognition differs across countries and times

questions.stem_md: Dev, a shopkeeper in the imagined Odrin market, plays a loudspeaker at full volume late at night to attract buyers, and nearby students cannot sleep. Using the idea of balancing rights, explain what should be done.
questions.solution_md: Clash, limit, mutual respect.

answer.model_answer_md: Dev's **freedom of expression and trade** clashes with the students' claim to **rest and study**. Rights are not absolute, so a **reasonable limit** such as no loudspeaker after a fixed hour or a lower volume should be set. Both sides then respect each other's rights.

marking_scheme.step: Identify the clash of two claims
A reasonable limit, such as fixed hours or lower volume
Both sides respect each other's rights

questions.stem_md: Explain three responsibilities of individuals that go with rights.
questions.solution_md: Three responsibilities.

answer.model_answer_md: First, individuals should **respect the rights of others**. Second, when their rights clash with those of others, they should **balance** the claims through reasonable limits. Third, they should **care for shared goods** such as the environment, since everyone depends on them.

marking_scheme.step: Care for shared goods such as the environment

questions.stem_md: Explain with an example why rights have reasonable limits, and say what makes a limit reasonable.
questions.solution_md: Why limits, an example, what makes them reasonable.

answer.model_answer_md: Rights have limits because using a right can harm others, for example a **procession** that blocks an ambulance route. A limit is **reasonable** when it protects the **rights of others or the common good**, is announced in advance, applies to all and leaves the right itself in place.

marking_scheme.step: Use of a right can harm others

questions.stem_md: Some argue that citizens should be vigilant when a government restricts rights in the name of security; others say that real threats may justify reasonable limits. State both views with a reason each, and suggest a test for judging a restriction.
questions.solution_md: Both views and a test.

answer.model_answer_md: Some argue that restrictions, once accepted, can **last or grow**, so citizens should watch them. Others argue that a real **threat** may justify limits for a time. A student can judge a restriction by asking whether it is **necessary, limited and open to review**.

marking_scheme.step: The other view with a reason
A test such as necessary, limited and reviewable

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of a right and its three sources.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and three sources.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **right** is a justified claim, recognised by society and usually by law, that lets a person live with dignity and freedom and places a duty on others.
2. **Natural rights** are said to be held by nature; Locke is linked with life, liberty and property.
3. **Human rights** belong to all persons because they are human; a United Nations declaration of 1948 is the best-known statement.
4. **Legal rights** are those that the law recognises and the state protects.
5. Constitutions often list legal rights, as the Indian Constitution does in its Fundamental Rights.

marking_scheme.step: Constitutions list legal rights, with an example

questions.stem_md: Describe the kinds of rights, with an example of each, and mention two newer claims.
questions.solution_md: Four kinds and newer claims.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Political rights** let people take part in government, for instance by voting, standing for office and forming parties.
2. **Civil liberties** protect personal freedom, such as speaking freely and receiving a fair trial.
3. **Economic rights** secure a livelihood, such as basic needs and a minimum wage.
4. **Cultural rights** protect a community's language and culture, including schooling in the mother tongue.
5. Newer claims, such as a **clean environment** and **privacy**, are increasingly recognised as rights.

questions.stem_md: Explain how rights place duties on the state and what responsibilities individuals have.
questions.solution_md: State duties and individual responsibilities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A right is a claim, so it places a **duty on the state**.
2. The state must **act**, by providing conditions such as schools and clinics.
3. The state must **refrain** from violating rights, for example by not arresting without lawful reason.
4. Individuals must **respect the rights of others** and balance their rights when these clash.
5. They should **care for shared goods** such as the environment.

marking_scheme.step: Rights place duties on the state
Respect and balance rights of others

questions.stem_md: Rights are not absolute. Explain this with an imagined clash of rights and the idea of reasonable limits.
questions.solution_md: Not absolute, an example clash, balance, what makes a limit reasonable.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Rights are **not absolute**, because using a right can harm others.
2. Imagine a neighbour in Pelham whose **loudspeaker** uses his freedom of expression and a student who needs **quiet** to study.
3. Each claim is valid, but neither can be used without limit.
4. A **reasonable limit**, such as fixed hours or lower volume, **balances** the two.
5. A limit is reasonable if it protects others and the common good, applies to all and is announced.

marking_scheme.step: Rights are not absolute, with a reason

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Quillon, three claims are made: (i) a sweet shop owner asks for free sugar every week; (ii) villagers ask for clean drinking water; (iii) one family asks that only its children may enter the town library. Apply the test of a right to each claim.
questions.solution_md: The three-part test applied to three claims.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A right is **needed for a dignified life**, accepted as **justified**, and can apply **equally to all**.
2. **Free sugar** is a want: it is not necessary for dignity and few could justify it.
3. **Clean drinking water** is necessary for health and dignity, can apply to all, and can be accepted as a right.
4. The **library claim** asks for a privilege for one family, so it cannot apply equally to all.
5. So only the claim to clean water passes the test.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the statement: rights can be enjoyed only when people also accept responsibilities. Use the idea of duties, the clash of rights and reasonable limits.
questions.solution_md: A weighed answer on rights and responsibilities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A right is a **claim on others**, so each right carries **duties**, for the state and for individuals.
2. If each person uses rights without respecting **others' rights**, rights clash and few can be enjoyed.
3. Individuals should **balance** clashing rights and **care for shared goods**.
4. **Reasonable limits** protect others and the common good, though citizens should watch that limits stay reasonable.
5. So the statement is largely sound: rights and responsibilities support each other, but the state also has duties.

marking_scheme.step: Clashes when others' rights are ignored

questions.stem_md: Read the debate extract and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined extract written by SOYL for practice; Pelham School and the speakers are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Bruno calls it a want.

**(b)** Needed and universal.

**(c) (i)** The test applied.

**OR (c) (ii)** A practical arrangement.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Bruno**.

**(b)** **Clean drinking water**, since it is needed for health and can be given to all.

**(c) (i)** A right must be **necessary for a dignified life** and apply **equally to all**. Bruno argues that the computer room can meet the need and not every school can supply laptops for all, so the claim **fails** the test and remains a want.

**OR (c) (ii)** The school could keep the **computer room** open longer or **lend** laptops for homework. This meets her need within the school's means and does not **harm the claims of others**.

Chetan said that clean drinking water at school is different: every child needs it for health, and it can be given to all. The moderator reminded the speakers that using a claim must not harm the claims of others.

answer.model_answer_md: **Bruno**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Suggest one way in which the school could meet Anika's need without calling a laptop a right, and give a reason.

questions.stem_md: Read the letter and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined letter written by SOYL for practice; Odrin, Esha and Dev are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Respecting others' rights.

**(b)** A reasonable limit.

**(c) (i)** Judgement with two reasons.

**OR (c) (ii)** Weighing both claims.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** To **respect the rights of others** (the student's rest and study).

**(b)** A **reasonable limit**, or balancing of rights.

**(c) (i)** Yes, it is largely reasonable. It lets Dev **keep his trade** during the day and evening, and it gives the student **quiet** at night. It is **announced** by a notice and applies to the whole lane.

**OR (c) (ii)** Dev's concern is real, so a limit should be **no wider than needed**. The student's claim to **rest and study** is also real. Fixed hours and a lower volume can protect both, and the reasons should be **explained to both sides**.

questions.stem_md: Read the meeting note and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined note written by SOYL for practice; the hamlet of Dunmere, its meeting and the people are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Shared goods.

**(b)** The state is asked to provide conditions.

**(c) (i)** A reasonable limit.

**OR (c) (ii)** Both, with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Caring for **shared goods** such as the environment.

**(b)** The request that the **district office provide the pit and a collection cart**.

**(c) (i)** The households claim freedom to use what they own, but dumping harms **everyone who depends on the stream**. Moving waste to a **pit** is a reasonable limit that protects the shared good while the households keep their freedom.

**OR (c) (ii)** On **both**. Villagers have a responsibility to **care for shared goods** and not to dump waste. The state has a duty to **act** by providing the pit and cart, since families alone may lack the means.
